To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the addition of a progesetin to an estrogen replacement regimen administered in a non-human primate model of women’s healt increases all anthropometric and computerized tomographic (CT) measures of obesity except for intra-abdominal (visceral) fat.

1) HRT increases total body fat and the deposition of fat in the subscapular and suprailiac skinfolds; 2) the addition of a progesin to the estrogen regimen increases total body fat but not fat deposition in the intra-abdmonal depot; 3) social status affects total body fat deposition and fat distribution patterns; and 4) the use of CT may measure fat distribution patterns differently than skinfold and circumferential measures.

The main takeaway from our work is that
CT may provide more sensitive measures of fat distribution in monkeys than skinfolds or circumferences.
CT scans can measure different characteristics of adipose tissue distribution than skinfilds or circumferences.
CT is a better tool to study fat distribution patterns than anthropometry, and that CT can detect changes in body fat patterns that are not apparent using anthropometry.
